---
title: "Case study: vaccination strategies on contact networks"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

A public-health team has doses for a fraction of a population and two ways to allocate them:

* **A, acquaintance immunisation** (Cohen, Havlin and ben-Avraham, 2003): pick a random
  person and vaccinate one of their contacts, until the doses run out. It needs only local
  information, such as asking people to name a contact.
* **B, degree targeting**: vaccinate the people with the most contacts. It needs the whole
  contact network.

Is the full information of B worth it, in the sense of reducing the final attack rate of an
epidemic by at least one percentage point? Experiments are simulations, each one cheap but
noisy; the question is when to stop simulating. The companion article runs the full study on
1,000 resampled streams with a known truth (`experiments/configs/app_epidemic_2026-10-23.R`).

```{r}
library(seqbench)
library(igraph)
```

## Simulating an epidemic

For an SIR epidemic with a fixed infectious period, the final set of infected people is the
union of the clusters of the index cases in *bond percolation*: keep each contact with
probability equal to the transmissibility `T`, remove the vaccinated, and take the connected
components that contain the index cases (Newman, 2002). That makes each simulation a few
milliseconds.

```{r}
final_size <- function(gp, vacc, ord, n_index = 5L) {
  keep <- !vacc
  memb <- components(induced_subgraph(gp, which(keep)))$membership
  idx <- match(ord[keep[ord]][seq_len(n_index)], which(keep))   # first unvaccinated in a shared order
  sum(memb %in% unique(memb[idx])) / length(vacc)
}

acquaintance <- function(adj, nd) {
  N <- length(adj); v <- logical(N); deg <- lengths(adj)
  while (sum(v) < nd) {
    r <- sample.int(N, 1)
    if (deg[r]) v[adj[[r]][sample.int(deg[r], 1)]] <- TRUE
  }
  v
}
```

## Instances and seeds

An **instance** is a network with its epidemic parameters, drawn from a population of
networks: Erdős-Rényi, Barabási-Albert or Watts-Strogatz, 500 to 1,500 people, basic
reproduction number between 1.5 and 3 and coverage between 5% and 20%. A **seed** is one
stochastic epidemic on that network. Both strategies see the same percolated network and the
same order of candidate index cases in a seed (common random numbers), so the losses are
paired by `(instance, seed)`. The loss is the attack rate, the fraction of the population
infected, so the bounds `[0, 1]` hold by construction.

```{r}
network_instance <- function(seeds = 3L) {
  N <- sample(500:1500, 1)
  g <- simplify(switch(sample(3, 1),
    sample_gnm(N, round(N * runif(1, 2, 6))),
    sample_pa(N, m = sample(2:4, 1), directed = FALSE),
    sample_smallworld(1, N, nei = sample(2:4, 1), p = runif(1, 0.01, 0.2))))
  deg <- degree(g); Tr <- min(1, runif(1, 1.5, 3) * mean(deg) / (mean(deg^2) - mean(deg)))
  nd <- round(runif(1, 0.05, 0.20) * N)
  el <- as_edgelist(g, names = FALSE)
  adj <- lapply(split(c(el[, 2], el[, 1]), factor(c(el[, 1], el[, 2]), levels = seq_len(N))), as.integer)
  t(vapply(seq_len(seeds), function(s) {
    va <- acquaintance(adj, nd)
    vb <- logical(N); vb[order(-deg, runif(N))[seq_len(nd)]] <- TRUE
    gp <- delete_edges(g, which(runif(ecount(g)) > Tr)); ord <- sample.int(N)
    c(seed = s, loss_a = final_size(gp, va, ord), loss_b = final_size(gp, vb, ord))
  }, numeric(3)))
}
```

Three seeds per network are fixed in advance. They are averaged by the package into one
observation per network; the network, not the simulation, is the sequential unit.

## Design and run

```{r}
design <- comparison_design(alpha = 0.05, margin = 0.01, bounds = c(0, 1),
                            boundary = "betting", n_max = 400)
set.seed(11)
state <- initialize_comparison(design)
k <- 0
while (stopping_decision(state) == "continue") {
  rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:10, function(i) cbind(instance = k + i, network_instance())))
  state <- suppressWarnings(update_comparison(state, as.data.frame(rows)))
  k <- k + 10
}
stopping_decision(state)
glance(state)
```

```{r}
ggplot2::autoplot(state)
```

## Reading the result

The report says how many networks and simulations were consumed and which assumptions the
decision rests on. Two features of these data are worth noticing, because they are typical of
simulation outputs:

* many paired differences are exactly zero, when both strategies stop the epidemic or both
  fail to, and the rest are skewed;
* simulations of the same network are correlated.

The betting boundary is valid under both: it assumes only that the losses lie in `[0, 1]`
and that networks are independent draws. A Gaussian confidence sequence assumes more, and the
companion article measures how its coverage degrades on exactly this kind of data. Feeding each
simulation as its own instance (pseudoreplication) would also be invalid: see
`vignette("seeds-and-refusals")`.

The answer concerns the **mean** over the population of networks. The benefit of degree
targeting depends strongly on how heterogeneous the contacts are, so a team that knows its
network is homogeneous, or scale-free, should define the population accordingly, and
pre-register any subgroup comparison as a comparison of its own.
